The cache is a Redis-backed, hash-versioned, per-workspace store fronted by an in-process map. Each entry is a provider class tagged with @WorkspaceCache(keyName, {packingPonderation, localDataOnly?}) (or @WorkspaceDerivedCache(name) for derived entries). Reads go through getOrRecomputeWithHashes, then a per-pod PromiseMemoizer, then a 100ms local-TTL check, then a Redis mget of the `<key>:hash` values. On mismatch the pod fetches `<key>:data` or recomputes via computeForCache. Recomputed data is published with a compare-and-set Lua script that only writes if the stored hash still equals the expected one. Pods share no pub/sub; they converge by comparing hashes. Derived entries are never stored: they are computed from a source entry (computeFromSource), memoized per source object in a WeakMap, and carry the source's hash. Invalidation (invalidate) writes a fresh random UUID to `:hash`, deletes `:data`, resets the local check timestamp, and clears the memoizer. invalidateAndRecompute then recomputes and republishes. In practice the trigger is WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.executeRun, which calls invalidateCache after commit (and after rollback). Its keys come from getFlatEntityMapsKeysToInvalidateForWorkspaceMigration, plus rolesPermissions when getDerivedCacheTriggers reports a role/permission change, and it bumps the metadata version when schema-affecting metadata changed. Other callers invalidate directly (for example WorkspaceManyOrAllFlatEntityMapsCacheService.invalidateFlatEntityMaps, row-level predicate group deletion, and upgrade commands). Caveat: other pods can serve a memoized result for up to MEMOIZER_TTL_MS (10s), since invalidation only clears the local memoizer. Also, getDerivedCacheTriggers does not list objectMetadata or row-level predicate maps even though rolesPermissions reads them; I did not confirm whether those changes are covered elsewhere.

Workspace metadata cache entries are declared with @WorkspaceCache(keyName, options) on WorkspaceCacheProvider subclasses (or @WorkspaceDerivedCache on WorkspaceDerivedCacheProvider subclasses) and registered in WorkspaceCacheService.onModuleInit. Reads go through getOrRecomputeWithHashes -> getOrRecomputeProviderEntries, which serves a per-pod local copy and revalidates it against a Redis hash every 100 ms (no pub/sub). Writes rotate the Redis hash to a random token and delete the data; recomputes publish through a compare-and-set Lua script. Derived entries have no Redis storage; they reuse their source's hash and memoize by source object identity. Invalidation is triggered by WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.executeRun, which calls invalidateCache after commit or rollback. invalidateCache expands touched keys and derived-trigger flags, calls invalidateAndRecompute, and bumps the metadata version via incrementMetadataVersion only for objectMetadata/fieldMetadata/index changes. flush() is a separate delete-only path with no recompute and no version bump.

answer.summary: Each workspace's metadata entries are declared with @WorkspaceCache (stored in Redis as <key>:<ws>:hash and :data) or @WorkspaceDerivedCache (computed in memory from a source entry, never stored). WorkspaceCacheService keeps a per-pod local copy and validates it against the Redis hash every 100ms; there is no pub/sub, and a 10s per-pod PromiseMemoizer can extend staleness. Schema and permission changes go through WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.invalidateCache after commit, which invalidates the affected flat-entity keys plus rolesPermissions and bumps the metadata version for objectMetadata/fieldMetadata/index changes; about 100 other call sites invalidate directly.

The workspace metadata cache is a two-tier store: a per-pod in-memory map (`localCache`) backed by Redis (`EngineWorkspace` namespace), with each key stored as a `:hash` and a `:data` entry. Keys are declared by a type entry in `WorkspaceCacheDataMap` (or `WorkspaceDerivedCacheDataMap` for derived keys) plus a provider class with `@WorkspaceCache(keyName, options)` (or `@WorkspaceDerivedCache(keyName)`); `WorkspaceCacheService.onModuleInit` discovers them via reflection. Reads go through `getOrRecomputeWithHashes`, which checks local TTL (100 ms), compares the local `latestHash` with Redis, and fetches data or recomputes via `computeForCache` and an atomic Lua compare-and-set publish. There is no pub/sub: pods converge by re-checking Redis hashes on read. Derived entries have no storage; they are computed in-process from a source key's data and memoized by source object identity, so they follow the source's hash and are never invalidated directly. After a committed migration, `WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService` calls `invalidateCache`, which invalidates the changed flat-map keys (plus `rolesPermissions`, `workflowAutomatedTriggerMaps`, `userApplicationVariableValueMaps` when triggered) and bumps the workspace metadata version when the change is schema-affecting. Non-migration writes call `invalidateAndRecompute` directly. Caveat: remote pods do not clear their per-process `PromiseMemoizer` (10 s TTL) on invalidation, so a pod may serve a memoized snapshot for up to ~10 s. That bound is inferred from the code, not measured.

Each cache kind is a class decorated with @WorkspaceCache(key, {packingPonderation, localDataOnly?}) (or @WorkspaceDerivedCache(key)) and discovered at startup via DiscoveryService; a stored entry is a Redis pair `${key}:${ws}:hash` (random token) and `:data` (compacted JSON) plus a per-pod local Map. Reads trust the local copy for 100 ms, then compare the Redis hash token and re-fetch or recompute on mismatch, so there is no pub/sub. Writes replace the hash token and delete data via msetAndMdel, then recompute and publish with a Lua compare-and-set on the expected hash. Derived entries (e.g. userWorkspaceRoleMap from flatRoleTargetMaps) are never stored: they reuse the source's hash and are computed in-process with a WeakMap memo keyed by source object. After a schema change (objectMetadata/fieldMetadata/index actions), WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.executeRun calls invalidateCache post-commit (and after rollback on error), which invalidates the changed flat maps plus flatFieldMetadataMapsOrm, adds rolesPermissions when permission maps or morph fields change, and then bumps the workspace metadata version. Caveat from reading the code: the per-process PromiseMemoizer keeps resolved results for 10 s and is cleared only locally, so another pod can serve a stale memoized result for up to ~10 s, not 100 ms. I did not fully trace the role-assignment write path to the runner, nor the sources of the other derived keys.

The workspace metadata cache is a WorkspaceCacheService with per-pod local maps backed by Redis. Each cache entry is a WorkspaceCacheProvider class decorated with @WorkspaceCache(keyName, options) that implements rowsRequirement and computeForCache. Derived entries are WorkspaceDerivedCacheProvider classes that compute from a source entry and have no Redis keys of their own; their hash is the source's hash. Pods stay consistent without pub/sub: Redis holds a random per-key hash that acts as the version, and each pod revalidates its local entry against Redis at most every 100 ms. Redis publishes are compare-and-set on the expected hash. Invalidation after a schema or permission change happens in WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.invalidateCache (post-commit and after rollback). It computes the affected keys, adds rolesPermissions, workflow trigger and application-variable keys via getDerivedCacheTriggers, calls invalidateAndRecompute, and bumps the metadata version only when object, field or index metadata changed. Other sites call invalidateAndRecompute directly, notably RowLevelPermissionPredicate services for rolesPermissions. evictWorkspaceFromLocalCache is pod-local only.

Each cache entry kind is a provider class registered via a decorator: a stored entry extends WorkspaceCacheProvider and uses @WorkspaceCache(keyName, {packingPonderation, localDataOnly?}), while a derived entry extends WorkspaceDerivedCacheProvider with @WorkspaceDerivedCache(key) and a sourceKeyName. WorkspaceCacheService.onModuleInit discovers both via DiscoveryService. Reads go through getOrRecomputeWithHashes → getOrRecomputeProviderEntries, which applies a 10s process-local memoizer, a 100ms local TTL, and a Redis hash comparison (`<key>:<ws>:hash`); on mismatch it fetches `:data` or recomputes via computeForCache and publishes with a Lua compare-and-set (PUBLISH_WORKSPACE_CACHE_SCRIPT). There is no pub/sub: pods converge because invalidation writes a fresh random hash and deletes `:data`, so each pod notices on its next revalidation. Derived entries (roleIdsWithAllRecordsAccess, userWorkspaceRoleMap, apiKeyRoleMap, flatRoleTargetByAgentIdMaps, graphQLResolverNameMap) have no Redis storage; they reuse the source's hash and memoize per source object in a WeakMap. Schema and permission changes are invalidated by WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.executeRun (post-commit and on rollback) → invalidateCache, which uses the affected flat-map keys, withDerivedFieldMetadataMaps, and getDerivedCacheTriggers (role/permission maps → rolesPermissions), then bumps the metadata version if the change is schema-affecting (objectMetadata/fieldMetadata/index). Other permission writers call invalidateAndRecompute(['rolesPermissions']) directly. Caveat: a non-originating pod can serve a memoized result for up to 10s because PromiseMemoizer is cleared only locally, bypassing the 100ms check.

Each workspace-scoped cache entry is a WorkspaceCacheProvider subclass tagged with @WorkspaceCache(keyName, options). Its computeForCache builds the value from rows loaded via rowsRequirement. WorkspaceCacheService discovers these providers at startup and serves reads from a per-pod in-memory Map, backed by shared Redis keys `<key>:<workspaceId>:hash` and `:data`. A pod reuses its local copy without checking Redis for 100 ms (LOCAL_TTL_MS). After that it compares its local latestHash with the Redis hash and either keeps the entry, loads the blob from Redis, or recomputes it. Publishing uses a compare-and-set Lua script, so a racing writer whose expected hash is stale is rejected and retried. Derived entries (@WorkspaceDerivedCache) are never stored: they are computed in-process from a source entry via computeFromSource and memoized per source object in a WeakMap, so they inherit the source's hash and are never invalidated directly. Invalidation (WorkspaceCacheService.invalidate) rotates the Redis hash to a new UUID, deletes the data keys, then recomputes. After a migration, WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.executeRun calls invalidateCache, which derives the keys from the touched flat-map keys plus triggers. Schema-affecting changes (objectMetadata, fieldMetadata, index) also bump the workspace metadataVersion. Role, role-target, object/field-permission and role-permission-flag changes invalidate rolesPermissions but do not bump metadataVersion. Some non-migration paths call invalidateAndRecompute directly (e.g. AccessGroupSyncListener, ApiKeyService.invalidateApiKeyCache).

Each cache entry is declared by a class decorated with @WorkspaceCache(keyName, {packingPonderation, localDataOnly?}) (stored) or @WorkspaceDerivedCache(keyName), and WorkspaceCacheService.onModuleInit discovers them via reflection. A read (getOrRecomputeWithHashes -> getOrRecomputeProviderEntries) checks the per-pod in-memory map (100ms freshness window), then compares the local hash with the Redis ':hash' key, and on mismatch fetches ':data' from Redis or recomputes from the provider's rows (WorkspaceCacheRowsBatchLoader); recomputes are published with a compare-and-set Lua script keyed on the expected hash. Pods coordinate only through Redis hashes: there is no pub/sub, and invalidation overwrites the ':hash' key with a random UUID and deletes ':data', so other pods notice on their next stale check. Derived entries (roleIdsWithAllRecordsAccess, userWorkspaceRoleMap, apiKeyRoleMap, flatRoleTargetByAgentIdMaps, graphQLResolverNameMap) are never stored: they reuse the source's hash and are computed in memory via getFromSource with a WeakMap keyed on the source object, so invalidating the source invalidates them. After a schema or permission migration commits, WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.executeRun calls invalidateCache, which picks keys from the actions via getFlatEntityMapsKeysToInvalidateForWorkspaceMigration and adds rolesPermissions and other derived-trigger keys from getDerivedCacheTriggers, then calls invalidateAndRecompute and bumps the metadata version when object/field/index metadata changed. Other direct callers (FieldPermissionService.upsertFieldPermissions, AccessGroupSyncListener, and many services) call invalidateAndRecompute or evictWorkspaceFromLocalCache for their own keys.

Each workspace cache key is a provider class decorated with @WorkspaceCache (or @WorkspaceDerivedCache for in-process derived values). WorkspaceCacheService discovers them at startup and serves reads through a per-pod memoizer, a local map trusted for 100 ms, Redis hash comparison, Redis data, and finally recomputation with a compare-and-set publish. Pods converge only by comparing the Redis `<key>:<ws>:hash` version pointer; there is no pub/sub, and other pods can serve memoized values for up to 10 s. Derived keys have no storage of their own and are invalidated through their source key. Schema and permission changes invalidate through WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.invalidateCache, which derives keys from the migration actions plus derived triggers (rolesPermissions, workflow triggers, app variables); schema changes also bump the Redis metadata version. RLS predicate changes and some object-metadata updates invalidate directly from their services, and the runner's rolesPermissions trigger does not cover the RLS maps.

Per-workspace metadata cache: each entry kind is a @WorkspaceCache-decorated WorkspaceCacheProvider (computeForCache + rowsRequirement), registered at startup by WorkspaceCacheService.onModuleInit. Reads go through getOrRecomputeProviderEntries, which uses a per-pod PromiseMemoizer (10s), a local map checked against Redis ':hash' keys every 100ms, and falls back to Redis ':data' or recompute, with a CAS publish script. Derived entries (@WorkspaceDerivedCache) are never stored; they are memoized per source object and share the source's hash. Schema changes invalidate via WorkspaceMigrationRunnerService.invalidateCache after commit (plus rollback), which bumps the metadata version only for object/field/index changes; permission changes invalidate rolesPermissions via getDerivedCacheTriggers or explicit callers. Caveat: cross-pod staleness can reach 10s via the memoizer, and failed post-commit invalidation is not retried.

answer.summary: The workspace GraphQL API is mostly NOT served by building a per-workspace GraphQL schema and running it through graphql-js. The fast path (DirectExecutionService, invoked from the useDirectExecution Yoga plugin) parses the request, looks up each top-level field name in a cached graphQLResolverNameMap (derived from flatObjectMetadataMaps via buildResolverNameMap), asserts args, and calls the resolver factory's create(context)(null, args, null, info) directly. The result is shaped to the selected fields with graphqlFields and graphQLFormatResultFromSelectedFields. Per-field errors become data[key]=null plus a formatted error; formatError maps domain exceptions through workspaceQueryRunnerGraphqlApiExceptionHandler, translates userFriendlyMessage with i18n, reports unexpected ones to Sentry, and falls back to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. Only introspection (__schema/__type) runs graphql-js execute over buildSchema of cached SDL. Generated-schema code is still used by: WorkspaceSchemaFactory.createGraphQLSchema (makeExecutableSchema with WorkspaceResolverFactory resolvers) for SDK client generation, and WorkspaceGraphqlSchemaSDLService.getOrComputeSchemaSDL/computeAndCacheSchemaSDL, which generates the SDL via WorkspaceGraphQLSchemaGenerator and caches it (one-week TTL, keyed by metadata hash and application id). ApplicationSchemaResolver returns that SDL as a string. Core (non-workspace) fields and subscriptions fall through to the static Yoga schema configured in GraphQLConfigService.createGqlOptions.

Workspace data operations (e.g. listing people, creating a company) are not run through a per-workspace GraphQL schema. Yoga's `useDirectExecution` plugin intercepts the request before the engine runs. It checks the root field names against a cached `graphQLResolverNameMap` (derived from the workspace's flat object metadata), and if they are workspace fields it dispatches each root field directly to a resolver factory (`DirectExecutionService.executeWorkspaceQuery` → `executeField`) and returns the response with `endResponse`, so no `graphql.execute` runs. Cached inputs are the flat object, field and index maps, served by `WorkspaceCacheService.getOrRecompute` (in-process TTL, then Redis hash-keyed, then recompute). Errors go through `DirectExecutionService.formatError`, which maps domain exceptions via `workspaceQueryRunnerGraphqlApiExceptionHandler` and localizes `userFriendlyMessage`. A SDL-based schema is built only for introspection fields (`executeIntrospectionQuery` calls `buildSchema` on a cached SDL from `getOrComputeSchemaSDL`). The generator path (`WorkspaceGraphQLSchemaGenerator.generateSchema`, then `printSchema`) fills that SDL cache on a miss. The executable-schema path (`WorkspaceSchemaFactory.createGraphQLSchema`) is used only by SDK client generation, not by the request path. Core (non-workspace) fields go to the NestJS code-first schema.

Workspace data operations (e.g. listing people, creating a company) are not executed by the GraphQL engine against a per-workspace schema. A Yoga plugin, useDirectExecution, runs in onRequest, parses the query, and dispatches each top-level field straight to the resolver factories with args taken from the AST, then returns the JSON response itself. The engine (graphql-js execute) is only used for introspection, and it runs against a schema built with buildSchema from the cached per-workspace SDL. Core (non-workspace) operations fall through to the normal Nest code-first schema. The per-workspace SDL is produced by WorkspaceGraphQLSchemaGenerator on a cache miss and cached under a hash of the metadata maps. Errors from the direct path go through DirectExecutionService.formatError, which maps known exceptions to GraphQL errors, translates userFriendlyMessage, and falls back to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. The generated executable-schema path (WorkspaceSchemaFactory.createGraphQLSchema) is no longer on the request path; it is only used by SDK client generation.

answer.summary: Workspace operations such as find-many people or create-one company are not served by executing a per-workspace GraphQL schema. A Yoga plugin, useDirectExecution, intercepts the request in onRequest, parses the query, and checks the root field names against a cached graphQLResolverNameMap (derived from the cached flatObjectMetadataMaps). If all root fields are workspace fields, DirectExecutionService runs each one directly through the same resolver factories (args assertion, then factory.create(context), then the resolver call) and returns JSON without calling the graphql execute engine, so argument checks are done by the assert*Args functions rather than graphql validation. Core-only queries fall through to the NestJS code-first schema built by GraphQLConfigService. Mixed core and workspace queries are rejected. The fast path depends on WorkspaceCacheService (in-process local cache with a 100ms hash check, then Redis hash/data keys, then recompute from providers) and on WorkspaceDerivedCacheProvider memoizing derived maps per source object. Errors are formatted per root field: a failed field returns null data plus a formatted error, domain exceptions are mapped to GraphQLError subclasses, userFriendlyMessage is translated, and unknown errors become INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. The generated-schema path (WorkspaceGraphQLSchemaGenerator to printed SDL, cached by hash) is still used for introspection (buildSchema on each introspection request), SDK client generation (WorkspaceSchemaFactory.createGraphQLSchema, which makeExecutableSchema's the SDL with the resolver factories), and the application schema resolver. It is not used for ordinary request execution.

Workspace operations (e.g. people listing, company creation) are not run through a per-workspace GraphQL schema by graphql-js. A Yoga plugin, useDirectExecution, runs in onRequest before Yoga's parse/validate/execute pipeline. It parses the query and checks the top-level fields against graphQLResolverNameMap, a workspace-cache entry derived from flatObjectMetadataMaps. If every root field is a workspace resolver, DirectExecutionService.executeWorkspaceQuery asserts the args, builds a resolver context from cached flat maps, calls the method's factory .create(context) and invokes the resolver directly. It then shapes the result by the selection set and ends the response with {data, errors}. Core-only operations fall through to the normal Nest code-first Yoga schema, and mixing core and workspace root fields is rejected. Because onRequest ends the response, Yoga's error and validation hooks do not run on this path. Per-field failures set data[field]=null and add a formatted error. formatError maps domain exceptions through workspaceQueryRunnerGraphqlApiExceptionHandler and graphqlDirectExecutionToGraphqlApiExceptionHandler, localizes userFriendlyMessage, captures unexpected errors, and falls back to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. The generated-schema path is still used for introspection (SDL to buildSchema), for SDL generation on cache miss (cached per metadata hash), for SDK client generation (WorkspaceSchemaFactory.createGraphQLSchema), and for the application-development schema resolver.

Workspace operations (e.g. listing people, creating a company) are not served by a per-workspace executable GraphQL schema on the hot path. Yoga's `useDirectExecution` plugin intercepts `/graphql` requests before validation and execution, parses the query with `graphql.parse`, and looks up each root field in a cached `graphQLResolverNameMap` built from the workspace's flat object metadata. It then calls the matching resolver factory directly with the field's args and a partial resolve-info, and shapes the result to the selected fields. Core-only operations fall through to Yoga's NestJS code-first schema, and mixed core+workspace queries are rejected. The generated-schema code path (`WorkspaceGraphQLSchemaGenerator` → `printSchema` SDL cached in the workspace cache storage, then `makeExecutableSchema` in `WorkspaceSchemaFactory`) is still used for two things: introspection queries (the SDL is re-parsed with `buildSchema` and run through `graphql.execute` on each such request) and SDK client generation. Errors go through `DirectExecutionService.formatError`, which maps known exceptions to `BaseGraphQLError` subclasses, translates `userFriendlyMessage` into the request locale, and returns anything unrecognised as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. Root-level limit violations fail the whole response, while per-field failures set that key to null and add an error.

Workspace GraphQL operations are not executed against a per-workspace GraphQL schema on the hot path. The /graphql Yoga server's first plugin, useDirectExecution.onRequest, parses the query, classifies top-level fields against the workspace's cached graphQLResolverNameMap, and for workspace fields calls prebuilt resolver factories directly (DirectExecutionService.executeWorkspaceQuery -> executeField -> factory.create(...)), then ends the response before Yoga executes. Core-only queries fall through to the static NestJS schema. The per-workspace SDL/schema generator (WorkspaceGraphqlSchemaSDLService / WorkspaceGraphQLSchemaGenerator) is only used on cache miss for introspection (buildSchema+execute per request) and SDK generation (WorkspaceSchemaFactory). Errors are mapped to BaseGraphQLError JSON per field via workspaceQueryRunnerGraphqlApiExceptionHandler, with i18n-translated userFriendlyMessage and Sentry capture.

Workspace operations (e.g. listing people, creating a company) are not normally run by graphql-js against a per-workspace schema. A Yoga plugin, useDirectExecution, runs in onRequest and answers the request itself. It parses the document, classifies each top-level field by looking it up in a cached resolver-name map built from the workspace's object metadata, and calls the resolver factories directly with the parsed args and a partial resolve-info. Field results are then pruned to the selection set. Only core fields, subscriptions, or unparseable requests fall through to the normal code-first Nest/Yoga schema. Metadata is served from the WorkspaceCacheService (process-local Map with a 100ms hash re-check against Redis, backed by Redis data and recompute from the DB). Errors are mapped per field via the workspace query-runner exception handler, with userFriendlyMessage translated, and unknown errors become INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. The generated-schema path (WorkspaceSchemaFactory → WorkspaceGraphQLSchemaGenerator → printSchema → makeExecutableSchema) is still used for introspection (buildSchema on cached SDL, no resolvers), for SDK client generation, and for the application-schema dev resolver. It is not used for normal workspace query execution.

The server does not build and execute a per-workspace GraphQL schema per request. Yoga is configured with a static core schema (autoSchemaFile, CoreEngineModule + ModulesModule). The useDirectExecution Yoga plugin intercepts workspace root fields, looks them up in a cached graphQLResolverNameMap (derived from flatObjectMetadataMaps), and DirectExecutionService calls the same resolver factories the generated schema would have used, field by field, without graphql-js validate/execute. Per-workspace SDL is generated on cache miss and cached (keyed by a hash of object/field/index/application metadata) for introspection; makeExecutableSchema (WorkspaceSchemaFactory.createGraphQLSchema) is only used by SDK client generation. Errors are mapped per field via workspaceQueryRunnerGraphqlApiExceptionHandler (domain exceptions to GraphQLError, others to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR), and core-field requests get formatting from useGraphQLErrorHandlerHook.

An update to a record is caught by WorkflowDatabaseEventTriggerListener.handleObjectRecordUpdateEvent. handleEvent loads the matching cached trigger listeners and, for each one, calls shouldTriggerJob. That checks the watched fields (eventMatchesWatchedFields) and the trigger's filter (eventMatchesRecordFilter, which calls evaluateStepFilters). Only when both pass does the listener enqueue WorkflowTriggerJob on workflowQueue. This is the first hand-off, picked up by WorkflowTriggerJob.handle, which resolves the core version and calls CoreWorkflowRunnerService.run. run creates the workflowRun as NOT_STARTED (not MANUAL, so not ENQUEUED), increments the not-started counter, and enqueues WorkflowRunEnqueueJob (second hand-off, cache mode). WorkflowRunEnqueueJob.handle calls WorkflowRunEnqueueWorkspaceService.enqueueRunsForWorkspace, which admits runs and calls enqueueRunOrFailIt. That enqueues RunWorkflowJob (third hand-off). RunWorkflowJob.handle sends the new run to startWorkflowExecution, which marks it RUNNING and calls WorkflowExecutorWorkspaceService.executeFromSteps on the trigger's nextStepIds. executeFromStep then runs the first action inline via executeStep, processes the result, and resolves the next step IDs with getNextStepIdsToExecute. The following step runs by direct recursion into executeFromSteps in the same job. Only when executedStepsCount exceeds MAX_EXECUTED_STEPS_COUNT (20) does it hand off again (fourth hand-off): continueExecutionFromStepInAnotherJob enqueues RunWorkflowJob with lastExecutedStepId, which RunWorkflowJob.resumeWorkflowExecution picks up. I did not trace the wait, delay, or retry hand-offs (scheduleStepRetry and the delayed-jobs queue), since they are not on this straight path.

The next step runs in the same job via recursive executeFromSteps; only if executedStepsCount exceeds 20 does continueExecutionFromStepInAnotherJob enqueue hand-off 4: RunWorkflowJob with lastExecutedStepId (worker RunWorkflowJob.resumeWorkflowExecution → getNextStepIdsToExecute → executeFromSteps).

The edit is handled in the API process by WorkflowDatabaseEventTriggerListener, which evaluates the trigger's watched-fields check and record filter (shouldTriggerJob) and enqueues WorkflowTriggerJob. That worker calls CoreWorkflowRunnerService.run, which creates the run as NOT_STARTED and enqueues WorkflowRunEnqueueJob. That worker's enqueue service pushes RunWorkflowJob, which starts the run and executes the trigger's first step(s) via WorkflowExecutorWorkspaceService.executeFromSteps. The next step runs inline in the same job; only after MAX_EXECUTED_STEPS_COUNT (20) is execution handed to a new RunWorkflowJob (lastExecutedStepId), which resumes via resumeWorkflowExecution. Queue hand-offs: (1) WorkflowTriggerJob, (2) WorkflowRunEnqueueJob, (3) RunWorkflowJob for the first step, (4) optional RunWorkflowJob continuation past 20 steps. The trigger filter is evaluated on the producer side in the listener, not in the worker. Note: I did not read processStepExecutionResult or getNextStepIdsToExecute in full; the next-step inline recursion is taken from executeFromStep's code.

An update to a record fires WorkflowDatabaseEventTriggerListener.handleObjectRecordUpdateEvent, which filters triggers by watched fields and the record filter, then enqueues a WorkflowTriggerJob (hop 1). WorkflowTriggerJob.handle validates the version and calls CoreWorkflowRunnerService.run, which creates a NOT_STARTED run and enqueues WorkflowRunEnqueueJob (hop 2). WorkflowRunEnqueueJob.handle delegates to WorkflowRunEnqueueWorkspaceService, which marks runs ENQUEUED and enqueues RunWorkflowJob (hop 3). RunWorkflowJob.handle runs startWorkflowExecution, which executes the trigger's nextStepIds (the first step) via WorkflowExecutorWorkspaceService.executeFromSteps. Each step's result then drives getNextStepIdsToExecute, and the next step runs in-process via recursive executeFromSteps. Only after 20 executed steps (MAX_EXECUTED_STEPS_COUNT) does it hand off again (hop 4) with RunWorkflowJob carrying lastExecutedStepId, which RunWorkflowJob.resumeWorkflowExecution picks up. All queue hand-offs use the workflowQueue. The trigger's field and record-filter checks run in the listener on the event side, before hop 1, not in any worker. I did not trace how the workspace event emitter delivers the update event to the listener.

Messages still linked to other channels and threads with live messages are protected. Deletes are hard; participants cascade with their message. Blocklist delete/update instead enqueue BlocklistReimportMessagesJob to reset channel sync. Caveats: SQL exact-address match is case-sensitive, and the own-address exclusion applies only to domain entries.

answer.summary: Adding a blocklist entry: MessagingBlocklistListener.handleCreatedEvent enqueues BlocklistItemDeleteMessagesJob, which re-reads the blocklist rows, groups them into workspace-scoped and member-scoped handles, and deletes messageChannelMessageAssociation rows for matching FROM/TO participants on the affected channels (domain entries match the domain and its subdomains, excluding the channel's own handle and aliases; exact-address entries have no own-address guard). It then calls MessagingMessageCleanerService.cleanOrphanMessagesAndThreads, which in one transaction deletes messages with no remaining channel association (and their attachments) and then threads with no remaining messages. Update and delete events also trigger BlocklistReimportMessagesJob, which marks channels for re-fetch so the import-side filter (isEmailBlocklisted) applies. Caveat: unescaped ILike wildcards in domain values.

When a blocklist record is created, MessagingBlocklistListener.handleCreatedEvent (triggered by the batched CREATED database event) enqueues BlocklistItemDeleteMessagesJob on the messaging queue, passing the event batch unchanged. That job re-reads the blocklist rows by recordId and splits them with groupBlocklistHandlesByOwner into workspace-scoped handles and per-member handles. For each group it loads the relevant message channels (all workspace channels, or only the member's connected-account channels) and calls deleteMessagesForMessageChannels, which finds participants with role FROM or TO (BLOCKLISTED_PARTICIPANT_ROLES) matching the handle. Exact emails match on equality; a domain entry (leading "@") matches via ILike '%@domain' or '%.domain', excluding the channel's own handle and handleAliases. It then deletes only the MessageChannelMessageAssociation rows for those messages on that channel. Afterwards cleanOrphanMessagesAndThreads scans the whole workspace by keyset pages and deletes messages with no remaining channel association (attachments first), then threads with no remaining messages, reconciling surviving threads' participant targets. Protection: a message still linked to another channel survives, domain matches never hit the channel's own addresses, and CC/BCC-only participants are untouched. UPDATED events run both the delete job and BlocklistReimportMessagesJob, and DELETED runs only the reimport job, which resets sync for affected channels so messages can be re-fetched. Import-time filtering uses isEmailBlocklisted/filterOutBlocklistedMessages. Notable gap: the exact-email delete path does not exclude the channel's own handle, unlike the domain path and the import-time check.

Flow for a new blocklist row (CREATED event): (1) The workspace event emitter dispatches a batch "blocklist.created" event, which MessagingBlocklistListener.handleCreatedEvent receives via @OnDatabaseBatchEvent. It does no work itself; it enqueues BlocklistItemDeleteMessagesJob on the messaging queue as a workspace job (only the delete job; the reimport job runs on DELETED and UPDATED). (2) BlocklistItemDeleteMessagesJob.handle runs in system workspace context, loads the blocklist rows by id, and groups them with groupBlocklistHandlesByOwner into workspace-scoped handles and per-member handles. (3) For each channel in scope (all workspace channels, or only the owner member's channels via their connected accounts), deleteMessagesForMessageChannels finds messageParticipant rows with role FROM or TO (BLOCKLISTED_PARTICIPANT_ROLES) that match the handle, then deletes the matching messageChannelMessageAssociation rows for that channel. Only the channel-message links are removed here. Domain entries ("@domain") match when the participant address ends with "@domain" or the domain ends with ".domain" (SQL ILIKE), and exclude the channel's own handle and handle aliases. Exact-address entries match on the handle directly, with no such exclusion in the SQL. (4) Then MessagingMessageCleanerService.cleanOrphanMessagesAndThreads runs workspace-wide, in a transaction, using keyset pages of 500. Messages with no remaining association are deleted, along with their attachments (when the targetMessage field exists). Threads left with no messages are deleted, and surviving threads are reconciled. Messages still linked to another channel are kept.
